A double check can be met only by moving the king. The only legal squares are g1 and h1; every other flight square is either occupied, attacked by the knight on f1, or still under fire from the queen.  

After the king steps to g1, the quiet follow-up c7h2 delivers mate. The queen attacks the king along the newly opened diagonal; the knight on f1 guards h2, preventing capture; and all remaining flight squares are covered by Black’s remaining pieces or are blocked by White’s own pawns. The identical mating move works if the king had chosen h1 instead.  

Thus the three-ply sequence g3f1 h2g1 c7h2 is forced mate in two.

(The same outcome occurs if White saves the rook instead; Black simply takes the bishop on the third ply.) This three-ply line therefore demonstrates the maximum material gain available from the fork.

The key tactical idea is a rook fork. White begins with d5e5, simultaneously attacking Black's queen on e6 and knight on e4. Black's only reasonable reply is to capture the rook with the higher-value piece (e6e5). White then plays d3d4, creating a second queen fork that attacks both the newly placed queen on e5 and the still-undefended knight on e4. Because the queen on d4 is protected twice (by the d1-rook and the e3-pawn), Black can capture it at most once; the remaining attacker falls on the next move, yielding a decisive material gain (queen for rook). This three-ply sequence is the forced continuation that realizes the fork motif.

The position features an absolute pin on White's bishop at c1 (Qa1 along the first rank to Kg1). Black is in check from Qc8 and must address it before exploiting the pin. The three legal ways to escape check while preserving the pin are Kg8-f7, Kg8-h7 and Be7-f8.  

Kg8-h7 is the safest king flight: it evades all immediate threats and does not allow White a checking capture that wins material. White's strongest reply is then Qc8xc4, removing a pawn. Because the c1-bishop remains pinned it cannot recapture or flee, so Black simply plays Qa1xc1 and nets a full piece.  

All other escape sequences either lose the Be7 for nothing or permit White a disruptive check; the chosen line therefore yields the largest material gain while directly demonstrating the pin.

Black’s first move places the bishop on g4; this simultaneously attacks the rook on f3 and pins it to the king because any movement of the rook would expose the king to check. The rook cannot capture the bishop (wrong movement direction for a rook) and no other white unit can capture on g4. Consequently the rook is lost.

White’s only legal way to break the absolute pin is to step the king off the diagonal; d3 is a representative safe square that does not allow an immediate follow-up check. Black then simply captures the undefended rook. The three-ply sequence therefore nets a full rook for nothing and is the clearest realization of the “Pin” motif.
